basis_note: Everything on this chart is the chance from ONE single occasion - one serving, one car trip, one meal, one hand of cards, one lottery ticket, one day. That matches how the food risks on this site are measured, so the comparison is like-for-like. Published odds are usually quoted per year or per lifetime, which are not comparable to a per-serving figure, so several anchors below were converted. Every conversion shows its arithmetic.
caution: These are still different kinds of event, and severity varies within each of them. A police-reported car accident ranges from a scraped bumper to something far worse, and cyclosporiasis ranges from a few days of upset to weeks of relapsing illness. The chart is here to give a feel for the size of a number like 1 in 100,000, not to claim the outcomes are equivalent.

anchors.label: Flipping ten heads in a row
anchors.note: Exact arithmetic: one half to the tenth power.

anchors.label: Getting food poisoning from any cause
anchors.derivation: CDC estimates 48 million foodborne illnesses a year in the U.S. Across about 342 million people eating roughly 3 meals a day, that is about 375 billion meals a year, giving roughly 1 in 7,800 per meal. The 3-meals-a-day figure is our assumption, not a CDC one.
anchors.note: All causes combined - bacteria, viruses and parasites - not Cyclospora alone.

anchors.label: Being dealt a royal flush
anchors.note: Exact arithmetic from a standard 52-card deck.

anchors.label: Being in a car accident
anchors.derivation: NHTSA recorded 6,138,359 police-reported traffic crashes in 2023, in which 40,901 people were killed, at a fatality rate of 1.26 deaths per 100 million vehicle miles travelled. NHTSA publishes that rate rather than a mileage total, so the mileage is recovered from it: 40,901 deaths at 1.26 per 100 million miles implies about 3,246 billion vehicle miles, which works out at about 189 crashes per 100 million miles. The 2022 National Household Travel Survey puts the average trip at about 13 miles, so one trip carries about 189 x 13 / 100,000,000, or roughly 1 in 41,000. Working it the other way round - 6.1 million crashes over the roughly 250 billion vehicle trips those miles imply - gives the same answer, because it is the same arithmetic rearranged. The published fatality rate is rounded to two decimal places, which is the loosest step here: taking it as anywhere from 1.255 to 1.265 moves the result only between 1 in 40,500 and 1 in 40,800, so the rounding does not reach the figure shown.
anchors.note: This counts any police-reported crash, from a bumper scrape upward, not just serious ones. It excludes minor collisions never reported to police, which some estimates suggest could be about as numerous again - if so the real figure is nearer 1 in 20,000. Both are shown rather than one, because the uncertainty is real.

anchors.label: Being struck by lightning
anchors.derivation: The National Weather Service puts the odds at about 1 in 1,222,000 in a given year. Spread evenly across 365 days that is about 1 in 446,000,000 on any one day. Spreading evenly is a simplification - lightning risk is concentrated in summer afternoons and in some states far more than others.
